One of the most powerful memory analysis tools available on Linux is Valgrind's Memcheck. Valgrind version 3.18.1 includes Memcheck, which can detect memory leaks, invalid memory accesses, and other memory-related errors. To use Memcheck, run your program with the `valgrind --leak-check=full ./myprogram` command, which will produce a detailed report of any memory issues found.

Another useful memory analysis tool is AddressSanitizer (ASAN), a compiler-based sanitizer that can detect a variety of memory errors such as out-of-bounds accesses and use-after-free bugs. To use ASAN, compile your program with the `-fsanitize=address` flag, then run it normally. ASAN will print detailed reports of any memory errors encountered.

The `/proc/meminfo` file provides a wealth of information about the current memory usage on your Linux system. This file reports metrics such as total available memory, free memory, cached memory, and swap usage. Analyzing the values in `/proc/meminfo` can help identify memory pressure and leaks at the system level.

For per-process memory usage, the `smaps_rollup` tool can provide detailed RSS (Resident Set Size) breakdowns. This tool analyzes the `/proc/<pid>/smaps` file to report the total RSS usage as well as the contributions from different memory regions like code, data, and shared libraries.

The `perf mem record` command from the Linux `perf` tool can be used to trace memory access patterns. This can help identify hotspots and potential performance bottlenecks related to memory access. The recorded data can be analyzed using the `perf report` command.

For more advanced memory tracing, the BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) framework can be leveraged. Tools like `bpftrace` and `eBPF` allow you to write custom programs that can instrument the kernel and capture detailed information about memory usage and access patterns.

The `jemalloc` memory allocator is a powerful alternative to the standard `glibc` allocator, providing advanced features for heap profiling and memory analysis. To use `jemalloc`, compile your program with the `jemalloc` library and set the `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` environment variable to control the number of arenas used.

Finally, the `massif` profiler, part of the Valgrind suite, can be used to generate detailed heap usage profiles.
